about.headline: Andy Ebert
story: Andy was born in West Berlin in November 1971, when the city was still divided by the Wall. Long before touring, live production, and professional sound engineering, his connection to music started at home.

His enthusiasm for music showed up early. He played every decorative—but very real—drum in his grandparents’ house and performed rockstar concerts on a plastic toy guitar. Not long after, he discovered a microphone his parents owned and began recording his voice onto cassette tapes.

After trying the organ and a few other instruments that failed to inspire him, Andy told his parents he wanted to play guitar. For his 10th birthday, he received a classical guitar and immediately began taking lessons.

Around the same time, he started buying his first rock and hard rock albums and fell in love with the sound of the electric guitar. It was the beginning of what would become a lifelong career in music.
Within months, he was playing with other musicians, borrowing an electric guitar, and learning what it meant to play in a band.

Inspired by friends whose fathers played guitar and owned recording equipment, Andy became interested in more than just playing music. He became fascinated by instruments, audio gear, and the process of recording.

He spent countless hours exploring the music stores of West Berlin with a drummer friend before buying his first Stratocaster and a small amplifier. After studying a book on home recording, he bought a six-channel mixer, a few microphones, and began experimenting.

That small collection of gear, combined with a tape deck, became the first version of his studio. In his parents’ basement, he recorded his band's first demo while the band also used the space for rehearsals. It was simple, live-to-tape home recording—but it was the beginning of something much bigger.

Eventually, the band needed a vocal PA for rehearsals and shows. Andy sold the six-channel mixer and upgraded to a 12-channel mixer with built-in power amps and a pair of wedges, which also became part of their live PA.

At 15, an internship at a music store—and his parents’ desire for him to receive a “real” education—led him into an apprenticeship in musical instrument retail. His customers ranged from beginners to professional musicians.

During those years, his basement studio continued to grow, adding a second recording room, a separate control room, and expanding to a 12-input / 8-output mixing desk and 8-track tape machine. Later, he upgraded again to a 24-channel console, a 16-track half-inch tape machine, and an expanding collection of microphones and outboard gear.
Music was no longer just a hobby. It was growing into a career.
In 1995, Andy changed jobs and began working in wholesale for Sonor Drums and Zildjian Cymbals.

In his spare time, he started mixing front of house for a friend's band—his first experience as a live sound engineer. His boss at Sonor also owned a local sound and lighting company, giving Andy the opportunity to work shows after hours and on weekends while continuing to record bands in his studio.
On January 30, 1997, Andy began his first professional touring job as a front-of-house engineer.

He toured with the Golden Gospel Singers and their band, playing primarily in churches throughout Germany and neighboring countries. Mixing a loud band in challenging church acoustics with limited speaker systems was a crash course in learning by doing.

After that tour, Andy began working as a backline technician and eventually joined TSE, a large audio company in Berlin. His work expanded to include sound engineering, PA and stage work, corporate events, hotel conferences, and concerts.

The variety of work gave him experience with everything from podium microphones to large-scale live productions. It also led to more opportunities mixing monitors at larger events—a role he quickly developed a reputation for.
The basement and his side hustle had taught him the basics of audio. The road taught him how to use those skills in live sound — do it all in one day, with no second chance that night.
National and European tours as a monitor engineer followed.

In the spring of 1999, Andy embarked on his first arena tour, mixing monitors for one of Germany's biggest pop acts, Modern Talking. That tour eventually led to a connection with Rocksound, the Scorpions' sound company.

The Scorpions' World Wide Live video had originally inspired Andy to become a sound engineer when he first watched it in 1985. In 1999 he actually worked with Achim, the Scorpions’ FOH engineer — the man he had admired in that video. One night at the hotel bar, Andy soaked up his stories and picked up new skills and techniques just by watching him work.

Touring with Rocksound and working for larger audio vendors throughout Germany helped establish his reputation. Eventually, Audio Rent / Clair Europe began hiring him for tours as both a monitor engineer and monitor technician, often working with American artists.
On many occasions, Andy found himself filling in for—or replacing—the tour's monitor engineer for the rest of the run.

In 2003, on his first trip to Los Angeles, Andy immediately fell in love with the weather, the people, and the music scene. More importantly, he met people who would continue to shape both his career and his life.
After that, Puddle of Mudd sponsored his first U.S. work visa.
What began in a basement in West Berlin had become an international career.
about.philosophy: At some shows I was allowed to mix the monitor sound. That was another incisive occurrence in my life and I knew — that is what I want to carry on with! I already knew a little bit about the psychology of mixing monitors, but I couldn't imagine that there would be a Mr. Bohlen who would primarily be responsible for my knowledge growing as much and as quickly as it did.
about.travel: To be a monitor engineer for Rocksound at the world exhibition Expo 2000 I had to move to Hannover for five months. Directly afterwards I toured for four months through half of Europe with a Gospel show again. In summer 2001 I worked for different companies at a couple of big festivals in Germany as local monitor engineer where I had the honor to mix the sound for some of my (teenage year) heroes.
about.behindTheScenes: From then on it was a fast way up. As well as my work at TSE I was touring as a backliner for some German artists and at some shows I was allowed to mix the monitor sound. Since Audio Rent I've been working with the most respected FOH engineers, production managers and tour managers worldwide.
funFacts: First guitar on his 10th birthday — Rock 'N' Roll for life
First live sound job as FOH in 1995; Golden Gospel Singers tour in early 1997
First major professional PA load-in: early Robbie Williams solo show, spring 1998
Monitor engineer for Modern Talking, 1999; Audio Rent – Clair Brothers Europe from 2002

media.biography: Andy Ebert is a Monitor and FOH Engineer based in worldwide touring production. Since going on the road in 1997, he has mixed monitors for artists including Alanis Morissette, The Weeknd, Maroon 5, Guns N’ Roses, Mariah Carey, Stone Temple Pilots, Neil Young, Velvet Revolver, Carrie Underwood, Adam Lambert, R.E.M., Dream Theater, and many others. He was nominated for the 2017 Parnelli Award for Monitor Engineer of the Year.
